messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus

Marcus was twenty-one when the convoy was hit. He had been a bus driver for only eight months before enlisting—a job his father had held for thirty years—and he'd imagined military service would be straightforward, disciplined, the kind of work that built character. He was stationed near Kandahar, riding in the third vehicle of a supply run on a Tuesday morning in June. The blast came from the roadside, a shape-charge IED buried beneath packed earth. The explosion tore through the vehicle ahead of him, and Marcus watched the truck lift and fold as if made of paper. The smell came next—acrid, chemical, underneath it something else that his mind couldn't quite name. When the helicopter arrived to evacuate the wounded, the percussion of its rotors seemed to shake his ribs. He remembered fragments: the screaming of the sergeant beside him, the taste of dust in his mouth, the feeling of his own body being too small to contain what was happening. But the pieces didn't connect. He couldn't construct a coherent sequence. When he tried to speak about it in the medical tent, the words simply weren't there—he knew what he'd seen, but the bridge between the knowing and the telling had collapsed.

Marcus returned to the States in September and moved back into his childhood home in Portland. For the first few weeks, he slept most of the day, then spent his nights on his phone, scrolling through games and videos, anything that kept his mind moving forward in small, manageable increments. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that danger lurked in ordinary places—a belief that made perfect sense to him given what he'd witnessed. The conviction that he had to remain on guard at all times, watching for threats, became almost a moral imperative. When his mother asked him to go to the grocery store with her in early October, Marcus felt his chest tighten at the thought of the crowds, the enclosed space, the potential for something to go wrong. He declined. He began to avoid shopping centres altogether, and when his sister invited him to a community event at church—their family's tradition since childhood—he refused so firmly that his mother stopped asking. The world, in Marcus's mind, was a dangerous place, and the safest thing he could do was contract his life to smaller and smaller spaces.

But the memories wouldn't stay contained. At random moments—a car backfiring, the sharp crack of a construction site jackhammer—the film would start playing again. Not a coherent narrative, but fragments in rapid succession: the metallic taste, the roar, a face he couldn't quite place. These intrusions terrified him because they felt like proof that he was losing his grip on reality. The fragmented, disjointed nature of the memories made him feel as though something inside him was broken in a way he couldn't repair. To manage this sense of disintegration, Marcus retreated further into his phone. He'd discovered that if he stayed engaged with games—the kind that demanded constant, low-level attention—the memories couldn't quite break through. He'd play for six, seven, eight hours at a stretch, his thumbs moving automatically, his mind in a kind of suspended state. When he wasn't gaming, he scrolled through social media, though the activity left him feeling hollow. His former supervisor called twice about returning to work at the transit authority; Marcus didn't call back.

By November, the cycle had tightened considerably. The fragmented memories—those disconnected pieces that felt like they belonged to someone else—had begun to reinforce his conviction that the world was dangerous and that he himself was fundamentally damaged. If his own mind couldn't hold the story together, how could he trust anything? This sense of untrustworthiness extended outward: he couldn't trust his perception, couldn't trust other people not to hurt him, couldn't trust that staying vigilant would actually keep him safe. The harder he tried to avoid triggers—he'd stopped taking certain routes home, avoided anywhere he might encounter crowds or helicopters from the nearby military base—the more his life contracted. And each contraction fed the memories, because avoidance itself became evidence that danger was real, that his hypervigilance was justified. The phone became his primary refuge. When his father found him at three in the morning, still gaming, still avoiding sleep, still trying to outrun the fragments, something shifted. His father recognized the look—the thousand-yard stare, the tremor in his hands—and finally insisted that Marcus speak to someone.

Marcus arrived at the clinic in early December, exhausted and uncertain whether talking could possibly help. What frightened him most was the possibility that if he stopped running—if he put the phone down and actually tried to speak about what had happened—the memories would overwhelm him entirely. But he was also aware, somewhere beneath the fear, that he couldn't keep living like this. He wasn't sure his life was worth living anymore, not in any way that resembled the future he'd imagined. He came because his father made him come, but also because some part of him, however small, recognized that the only way forward was to turn and face the thing he'd been running from.
